REVEILLE RESOURCES PLC

Chairman Interview

Reveille [AQSE: REV], a uranium exploration and development company with a primary focus on Italy's largest uranium deposits, announces that its Non-Executive Chairman, The Hon. Michael R. Pompeo, former US Secretary of State and CIA Director, has participated in an interview with Jeremy Naylor.

Notes to Editors

Reveille Resources plc (AQSE: REV) is a UK natural resources exploration and development company with a primary focus on Italy, where it is advancing the exploration and development of the country's largest historic uranium deposits.

Through its Italian subsidiary, Futuro Energetico Italiano S.r.l, the Company has submitted exploration-licence applications in respect of the Novazza and Val Vedello uranium projects in northern Italy, each of which is subject to the applicable environmental-assessment process. The projects were historically explored and developed by AGIP Nucleare S.p.A. and its operating subsidiary, SOMIREN, both part of the ENI group, during Italy's national nuclear programme between 1959 and 1983. This work included more than 87,000 metres of historical drilling and approximately 17 kilometres of underground development.

Reveille's strategy is to identify and advance uranium projects that have benefited from substantial historical exploration and technical work, but where value has yet to be fully realised due to geopolitical, technological, financial or historical factors. By applying modern exploration techniques and internationally recognised reporting standards, the Company intends to verify historical data, advance exploration and work towards the delineation of mineral resources in accordance with internationally recognised reporting standards.

While Italy remains the Company's principal area of focus, Reveille will selectively evaluate additional uranium opportunities elsewhere in Europe and in other Western jurisdictions where similar value creation opportunities exist. The Company is committed to advancing its projects responsibly, working closely with local communities, regulators and other stakeholders to ensure that exploration activities are undertaken to the highest environmental, technical and governance standards.

data.title: Bank of Canada to raise rates to 2.50% on October 28 and once again by end-March
data.description:
By Nushaiba Iqbal

The Bank of Canada will raise its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28 and follow with one more hike by the end of March to pre-empt any further rise in inflation expectations, according to a majority of economists polled by Reuters.

Inflation rose to 3.1% in September, only barely overshooting the BoC's target range of 1% to 3%. But the central bank's latest business outlook survey showed sharply rising inflation expectations in the run-up to a recent breakdown in trade talks with the United States, Canada's main export destination.

Quarterly inflation forecasts from the bank, also due next week, are likely to be revised higher, BoC Governor Tiff Macklem told reporters in remarks Saturday that markets interpreted as a hint a rate rise is coming.

Interest rate futures have moved from pricing in a 30% chance of a rate hike in October to around a three-in-four likelihood. Many economists this week changed their view from a hold to a hike, citing those remarks from Macklem.

"What changed the tone in the governor's public comments on the weekend and what changed our view on Monday is the same source, and that is the responses from the BoC's business outlook and consumer surveys," said Royce Mendes, managing director and head of macro strategy at Desjardins.

"So presumably the governor had seen the results before they were published more broadly on Monday. And I would assume that informed his public commentary," Mendes said. "The survey responses...suggest there are more serious inflationary pressures coming."

Nineteen of 34 economists surveyed in the October 21-23 poll, or 56% of them, said the BoC will hike its overnight rate by a quarter percentage point to 2.50%, its first move in a year.

This is a clear reversal from the previous poll, when 80% of respondents forecast the bank would hold its rate at 2.25% until the end of 2026, and two-thirds of them forecast a hold until the end of March 2027.

Those economists who forecast no move next week mainly cited a weak economy and subdued inflation pressures despite soaring oil prices , which hit $117 a barrel for the first time since May on Friday.

Sixteen of 29 respondents, a 55% majority, also forecast one more rise before March 2027, after which policymakers would hold the overnight rate at 2.75%, poll medians showed. If correct, it will be the shortest BoC policy tightening campaign in 30 years.

But even a short series of hikes would bring the BoC into a widening group of central banks that have opted for tighter monetary policy in response to persistent inflation emerging as a result of the US-led war with Iran that began in February.

Among major central banks, only the BoC and the Bank of England — which is widely expected to raise rates at its early November meeting — have not yet begun to raise rates.

But many say the BoC will need to be measured with the pace of rate increases given other risks to the economy.

Benjamin Reitzes, Canadian rates and macro strategist at BMO, said: "They'd rather make the mistake of hiking a little bit too early, which means maybe they have to hike a little bit less at the end of the day than falling behind the curve, which is what happened in 2021-2022, and they don't want to repeat that mistake.”

Economic growth likely slowed to 1.9% last quarter from 3.3% in Q2 and is forecast at 1.3% in the current one before accelerating next year, poll medians showed. The economy will grow 1.0% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027, the survey found.

Inflation will average 2.8% for 2026 as a whole, falling to 2.3% in 2027, poll medians showed.

(Other stories from the Reuters global economic poll)

data.title: Novartis U.S. Shares Fall After MS Pill Trial Data Disappoint
data.description:
By Adria Calatayud

Novartis's U.S. shares fell after the Swiss drugmaker reported results of two late-stage studies of its multiple sclerosis pill that showed a reduction in flare-ups below that achieved by a rival drug from Roche Holding.

American depositary receipts in Novartis fell as much as 4.5% in U.S. midday trading Friday before recovering somewhat, reducing their year-to-date gains.

Novartis said its drug, known as remibrutinib and marketed as Rhapsido for skin condition chronic spontaneous urticaria, met the primary goals of the studies by reducing relapse rates relative to Sanofi's rival treatment Aubagio in patients with relapsing MS, the most common form of the disease. The results were presented at scientific congress MSToronto2026 in Toronto and published in medical journal the Lancet.

The studies showed the drug achieved reductions in the annualized relapse rate of 35.2% and 31.2% compared to Aubagio, the company said. This translated into one relapse every 13 years, it added.

No liver safety signal was observed, Novartis said.

Novartis, which was recently hit by trial failures of cholesterol and neuromuscular drugs, already reported initial findings from the studies last month, but analysts said a look at the full data was required to assess how its drug performed against the competitor product from Roche.

Roche, Novartis's Swiss cross-town rival, previously said its own multiple sclerosis pill, fenebrutinib, lowered the annualized relapse rate by 51.1% and 58.5% in two late-stage studies, but its drug showed signs of potential liver injury.

Analysts at UBS had said before Novartis released the full study data that the company would likely need to deliver efficacy data at least on par with Roche's fenebrutinib with a clean safety profile to trigger a positive market reaction.

Novartis said there were no cases that would raise concerns about drug-induced liver injury in its trials. Roche reported a case of potential liver damage.

By combining high efficacy with a favorable safety profile, the medicine has the potential to support long-term disease management, Novartis Chief Medical Officer Shreeram Aradhye said.

data.title: Energy Department Authorizes SPR Release to Deal With Supply Issues at Phillips 66 Lake Charles Refinery — OPIS
data.description:
The Department of Energy on Friday said it is releasing up to 400,000 bbl of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to help deal with an oil supply disruption affecting the Phillips 66 Lake Charles Refinery in Louisiana.

The department's announcement did not specify the nature of the disruption at the 264,000 b/d refinery.

"The supply will help offset temporary disruptions affecting crude oil deliveries to the refinery and support continued production of transportation fuels serving Louisiana and surrounding markets," the announcement said.

In a statement, Phillips 66 said it would not comment on refinery operations or commercial activity, but it did confirm the company will receive crude from the reserve.

"We do not anticipate impacts to Lake Charles operations," the company statement said.

The DOE announcement said the department had authorized release of the oil as an exchange, meaning Phillips will have to return the same amount of oil it receives, along with additional barrels as a premium for the loan.

That is the same type of arrangement the department has been using in its most recent program of releases from the reserve. DOE data this week showed supplies in the reserve now total 282.7 million bbl, the lowest levels since October 1982.

In recent weeks, the department has solicited bids for the loan of an additional 57 million bbl from the reserve, part of the Trump administration's efforts to deal with disruptions to global crude supply due the fighting in Iran.

So far, the department has not announced any agreements to release oil under the latest solicitations.

data.title: RBI alert about AI-driven cyber risks, banks taking steps to plug vulnerabilities: Sanjay Malhotra
data.description:
RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Friday said the central bank and other banks are alert about emerging cyber risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents and are taking measures to identify and plug vulnerabilities in their IT systems.

Referring to reports of AI agents operating in test mode that allegedly attacked banks overseas and stole data, Malhotra said such risks were real but could be addressed by keeping banking systems secure.

There are reports that major US banks have detected third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, raising concerns that automated tools could act beyond instructions given by customers.

"Our banks, the government as well as the RBI, we have alerted them, and they are conscious about it and they are taking measures to ensure that such kind of vulnerabilities, wherever they are, are plugged," he said at the NDTV World Summit.

The statement comes in the backdrop of the State Bank of India (SBI) acknowledging suspected exposure of 3,897 customer records with personally identifiable information on the dark web.

The RBI Governor said the central bank has a strong team, appropriate regulations and supervisory mechanisms, along with experts who audit the IT systems of major banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs).

The RBI is in continuous dialogue with banks and NBFCs to strengthen their IT infrastructure and ensure compliance with the prescribed regulations, he said.

Malhotra said the focus is on two key areas — data security and protection against cyberattacks – that could disrupt banking systems and cause downtime.

While the RBI has a robust regulatory and supervisory framework, the rapid pace of software development means that vulnerabilities can sometimes emerge, he said.

"It is our endeavour that we identify these vulnerabilities as soon as possible and plug them through the patches that have to be deployed in these IT systems,” he added.

On the FCNR deposit repayment, Malhotra said, the RBI has sufficient reserves and time to pay back the foreign currency non-resident (bank) deposits it garnered under its special concessional window.

“I am very optimistic that our external sector is very resilient, very strong. We already have sufficient money and reserves to pay that, but we will have even more than that. And the average deposit size is four years plus, so we have sufficient time to repay,” he said.

On June 8, the RBI unveiled a facility under which it would bear the full hedging costs for banks raising fresh 3-5 year FCNR(B) deposits, which closed on August 31, a month ahead of the original deadline.

The RBI received USD 132.98 billion worth of FCNR(B) deposits under the scheme.

Malhotra expressed confidence that India's external sector is very strong in the medium-term.

"I am optimistic that in the medium term the balance of payments and the external situation is going to be strong," he said.

"We already have sufficient forex reserves by all metrics. We built on them, we reinforced them, through the FCNR(B) scheme as you are aware. All other parameters, like services exports, remittances, among others, also point to a strong external sector in the medium-term,” he added.

data.title: Fast-fashion group Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle US FTC probe
data.description:
Key points:
  • Settlement equals nearly half of second-quarter profit
  • FTC has received 12,000 complaints about Shein since 2020
  • Regulatory headwinds in EU, US have slowed e-commerce growth

By Helen Reid and Jody Godoy

Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle an investigation by the US Federal Trade Commission over delivery delays and other customer complaints, a source with direct knowledge told Reuters on Friday.

The settlement, equivalent to 44% of Shein's second-quarter profit, is the latest to hit the online fast-fashion retailer facing a regulatory and tax crackdown in Europe and the US that has slammed the brakes on its growth.

Shein, founded in China though headquartered in Singapore, said in a statement to Reuters that it had "reached a constructive outcome with the FTC", and that additional information would be shared soon. An FTC spokesperson declined to comment.

The company had warned in July filings for its Hong Kong IPO that the US probe could lead to significant fines.

Consumers filed more than 12,000 complaints about Shein over more than $11 million in purchases between January 2020 and June 2026, according to FTC records reviewed by Reuters.

At least some of those relate to shipping, with customers reporting to the FTC and Better Business Bureau that they never received packages that Shein had marked as delivered, and that Shein customer service did not resolve the issue.

Reuters was not able to independently verify the substance of the complaints, or whether they were ultimately resolved.

As well as selling its own-brand clothing, Shein's website also operates as a marketplace where third-party sellers offer everything from toys to household appliances and decor.

MORE PAIN AHEAD FOR SHEIN WITH HIGHER EU FEES

Shein shares have already dropped 22% from their September 1 listing price as investors realised the extent to which the European Union's €3 fees on low-value e-commerce packages have bruised its business there.

And there's further pain ahead for Shein, with the EU imposing an additional €2 handling fee from November 1, making the total fee €5 per separate customs code.

"The way these tariffs are implemented is extra punishing for Shein," said Mike Ryan, head of e-commerce insights at Smarter Ecommerce, who has tracked how Shein has dialled down its spending on Google Ads visibility in Europe.

Shein was known for selling $5 dresses and $10 jeans, but has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.

CEO Sky Xu said last month that Shein would develop more higher-priced brands in an attempt to boost profitability.

Shein is also still under investigation by the European Commission over illegal products on its marketplace. It was fined €150 million ($168 million) by France's data protection authority over the improper use of cookies last year.

It's not the first time the US FTC has taken action against online retailers over deliveries.

US firm Fashion Nova was fined $9.3 million in 2020 for failing to meet shipping promises to customers and giving them gift cards instead of refunds.

Crocs Inc-owned Hey Dude was also fined $1.95 million in 2023 for failing to notify customers of shipping delays and suppressing negative reviews.

($1 = 0.8928 euros)

data.title: The Week in Oil: Fears of U.S.-Iran Escalation Push Brent to $117
data.description:
By Giulia Petroni

Here is a look at what happened in oil markets in the week of Oct. 19-23 and what the focus will be in the days to come.

OVERVIEW: Oil prices are on track for another weekly gain on fears of renewed escalation between the U.S. and Iran after the midterm elections. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was around $117 a barrel in midmorning U.S. trade, while West Texas Intermediate was just below $103 a barrel.

MACRO: Rising energy costs are fueling concerns over inflation and interest-rate hikes. According to the FedWatch tool, traders broadly expect the U.S. central bank to leave interest rates unchanged next week, but they see a nearly 80% probability of a hike in December.

Meanwhile, consumer sentiment in the U.S. ticked lower in October, hovering near record-low levels, according to the University of Michigan's survey. Inflation expectations instead moved slightly higher.

GEOPOLITICAL RISKS: Fears that the U.S. could attack Iran after the midterm elections in early November are driving oil's rise this week. The U.S. has a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine expeditionary unit en route to the Middle East, while the military has moved some troops off bases in the region.

The buildup comes at a politically sensitive moment, with Israel's general election scheduled for Oct. 27 and the U.S. midterms a week later.

Tehran warned that a renewed U.S. and Israeli air campaign would prompt retaliation extending well beyond military targets. Iran threatened strikes on American bases and warships, as well as airports, pipelines and other civilian infrastructure in neighboring Persian Gulf countries.

At the same time, persistent attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and deadly strikes by Yemen's Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia are keeping the geopolitical risk premium high. The market's focus is less on how much oil is available today than on whether Middle East exports can be sustained if fighting intensifies again.

SUPPLY AND DEMAND: Kpler data show that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain 26% below prewar levels, with the seven-day average at 12.65 million barrels a day, compared with a baseline of 17.15 million. Continued attacks on shipping are sustaining a risk premium in both freight rates and crude prices. Yet total Middle Eastern oil supplies reaching global markets, excluding Iran, remain above prewar levels.

Meanwhile, shipment of Russian diesel could be headed for the U.S., according to vessel-tracking data, potentially signaling a return of direct fuel deliveries as U.S. President Trump seeks to expand Russian supplies to international markets.

WHAT'S AHEAD: Markets will turn to the Federal Reserve's policy meeting on Oct. 27-28 and the release of the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, on Oct. 29 for clues on the outlook for interest rates. On the energy front, next week's focus will be on any signs of a potential escalation between the U.S. and Iran, fresh data on crude and refined-product inventories, and developments in Russian diesel shipments.
